title: Delirium: Acute Brain Failure
bottomLine: Delirium is acute or fluctuating inattention and altered cognition or awareness caused by an underlying insult until proven otherwise. Treat the cause and environment first; benzodiazepines, routine restraints and reflex antipsychotics can worsen outcomes.
recognize: Fluctuation, impaired attention, altered arousal and abrupt change from baseline are more important than memory impairment alone.
Hypoactive delirium is easily missed because the patient may appear quiet rather than agitated.
Common causes include infection, medications, pain, urinary retention, constipation, dehydration, hypoxia, metabolic disturbance and withdrawal.
differentiate: Dementia is usually chronic and progressive with relatively preserved attention early; delirium is acute and fluctuating and can occur on top of dementia.
Depression can mimic cognitive impairment but does not usually produce fluctuating attention and arousal.
assessment: Establish baseline from collateral history; review new medications, anticholinergics, sedatives, pain, bowel and bladder status, hydration, oxygenation, infection and sensory impairment.
Use a validated delirium tool as part of assessment, not as a replacement for cause-finding.
workup: Target tests to likely causes; routine head CT has low yield without trauma, focal neurologic signs or unexplained prolonged reduced consciousness.
management: Correct causes, mobilize, orient, restore hearing and vision aids, protect sleep, hydrate and nourish, manage pain and minimize lines and restraints.
Choosing Wisely Canada recommends against benzodiazepines or sedative-hypnotics as first choice for insomnia, agitation or delirium in older adults.
Use antipsychotics only selectively for severe dangerous distress or agitation after reversible causes and non-drug measures, with explicit risk review.
medicationSafety: Anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, opioids, corticosteroids and polypharmacy can precipitate delirium; medication reconciliation is treatment.
redFlags: Inability to protect self or others
counselling: Explain to families that delirium is a medical syndrome and may fluctuate; familiar presence and orientation can help.
followUp: Document baseline, precipitant and recovery; persistent cognitive change after delirium deserves reassessment.
examTrap: Giving lorazepam to a restless hospitalized older adult before checking urinary retention, hypoxia, medications and infection.
oneLinePearl: Delirium is a symptom; find the insult before sedating the behaviour.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Hospital Medicine Recommendations

title: Cognitive Decline and Dementia
bottomLine: Diagnose dementia from acquired cognitive decline that interferes with independence after excluding delirium, depression and reversible contributors. Function and safety matter more than a screening score alone.
recognize: Memory, executive, language, visuospatial or behavioural change may predominate depending on dementia type.
Functional losses in finances, medications, driving, cooking or appointments often reveal clinical significance before basic activities of daily living fail.
differentiate: Delirium fluctuates acutely; depression may produce low motivation and cognitive complaints; mild cognitive impairment preserves overall independence.
Rapid progression, focal neurologic signs, early gait disorder, seizures or systemic features require a broader neurologic or medical differential.
assessment: Obtain collateral history with consent or appropriate authority; assess cognition, function, mood, hearing and vision, sleep, medications, substances, falls and safety.
Assess capacity for specific decisions rather than assuming global incapacity because of a dementia diagnosis.
workup: Use cognitive testing plus targeted CBC, electrolytes, renal function, TSH, B12 and other tests based on presentation; brain imaging when atypical, focal, rapid or otherwise indicated.
management: Address vascular risk, sensory impairment, sleep, exercise, social engagement and caregiver supports.
Use dementia-specific pharmacotherapy only when appropriate to subtype and stage and after discussing modest expected benefit and adverse effects.
For behavioural symptoms, find pain, delirium, environment, unmet need and medication triggers before antipsychotics.
medicationSafety: Choosing Wisely Canada advises against antipsychotics as first-line treatment for behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia.
Minimize anticholinergic burden and sedative-hypnotics and review driving and falls risk.
redFlags: Psychosis or aggression creating immediate danger
counselling: Discuss diagnosis and future planning at a pace the patient wants; support autonomy, advance care planning and caregiver needs.
followUp: Track function, safety, caregiver strain, medication benefit and harm, and capacity as decisions arise.
examTrap: Prescribing an antipsychotic first for new agitation in dementia without assessing pain, delirium, constipation, environment or medication causes.
oneLinePearl: In dementia, new behaviour is a symptom until unmet need or delirium is excluded.

title: Falls and Frailty: Multifactorial Risk
bottomLine: A fall is a clinical event, not a normal part of aging. Look for injury and acute cause first, then address medications, orthostasis, gait and balance, vision, feet and footwear, cognition, environment, osteoporosis and fear of falling.
recognize: Falls can be caused by syncope, infection, arrhythmia, stroke, hypoglycemia, dehydration or medication toxicity as well as chronic balance impairment.
Frailty is reduced physiologic reserve and predicts vulnerability to adverse outcomes; it should change treatment intensity and recovery planning, not justify therapeutic nihilism.
differentiate: A 'mechanical fall' should not be accepted without asking why the person fell.
Falls with amnesia or unwitnessed collapse may represent syncope or seizure.
assessment: Assess injury and head strike, anticoagulation, prodrome or loss of consciousness, orthostatic vitals, gait and balance, vision, footwear, cognition and home hazards.
Review benzodiazepines and Z-drugs, anticholinergics, antihypertensives, hypoglycemics and other fall-risk-increasing drugs.
workup: Use ECG, labs or imaging based on acute cause and injury risk; do not order broad neuroimaging for every fall without indication.
Assess fracture risk and bone health rather than waiting for a hip fracture.
management: Treat the acute cause and injury, deprescribe or adjust contributory medicines, prescribe strength and balance training and address vision, footwear and environmental risks.
Avoid physical restraints as a fall-prevention strategy because they can increase injury and functional decline.
medicationSafety: Choosing Wisely Canada highlights benzodiazepines and sedative-hypnotics as major fall and fracture risks in older adults.
Deprescribing requires tapering where withdrawal is possible.
redFlags: Hip fracture or inability to weight bear
Recurrent falls with rapid functional decline
counselling: Use collaborative language: fall prevention aims to preserve independence, not restrict activity.
followUp: Reassess after medication changes and interventions and refer to PT, OT, a falls clinic or home assessment when needed.
examTrap: Telling an older adult to be more careful without reviewing medications, orthostasis and gait.
oneLinePearl: Every fall asks two questions: what happened today, and what makes the next fall likely?

title: Polypharmacy and Deprescribing
bottomLine: Polypharmacy becomes problematic when medicines lack indication, duplicate therapy, cause harm, conflict with goals or have time-to-benefit longer than the patient's priorities or life expectancy. Deprescribing is monitored treatment.
recognize: Medication harm can present as falls, delirium, constipation, urinary retention, orthostasis, bleeding, AKI, hypoglycemia and functional decline.
Transitions of care are common points for duplicate, restarted or unintentionally stopped medications.
differentiate: Do not stop a medication solely because it appears on a high-risk list; assess indication, benefit, alternatives and patient goals.
Preventive medicines have different time-to-benefit than symptom-control medicines.
assessment: Create a best possible medication history including OTC products and supplements; for each drug ask indication, effectiveness, harm, adherence, goals and monitoring.
Assess renal and hepatic function and anticholinergic and sedative burden.
workup: Use labs and vitals required to safely continue or taper high-risk therapies rather than ordering routine panels unrelated to the medications.
management: Prioritize stopping or tapering drugs with no indication or clear harm, one change at a time when possible, and monitor for withdrawal or recurrence.
Choosing Wisely Canada recommends against long-term risk-reduction medicines when life expectancy is shorter than the medication's time to benefit.
medicationSafety: Benzodiazepines, PPIs, antipsychotics, hypoglycemics, antihypertensives and antithrombotics are common review targets but require individualized plans.
Do not abruptly stop drugs with physiologic dependence or rebound risk.
counselling: Frame deprescribing as optimizing treatment, not giving up, and ask which outcomes matter most to the patient.
followUp: Document what stopped, why, how to monitor and ensure all prescribers and the pharmacy receive the updated list.
examTrap: Adding a medication to treat a side effect of another medication without first considering a prescribing cascade.
oneLinePearl: The safest drug may be the one with no remaining reason to exist.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Pharmacist, Hospital Pharmacy and Geriatrics Recommendations

title: Palliative Symptoms: Treat What the Patient Feels
bottomLine: Palliative care can be provided alongside disease-directed treatment. Match therapy to the patient's goals and symptom mechanism: opioids are appropriate for many pain and refractory-dyspnea situations, while oxygen is not routinely useful for non-hypoxic dyspnea.
recognize: Common symptom clusters include pain, dyspnea, nausea, constipation, anxiety, delirium, fatigue and secretions.
The same symptom can have reversible causes worth treating if doing so aligns with goals, such as urinary retention, constipation, effusion, infection, hypercalcemia or medication toxicity.
differentiate: Palliative intent does not mean do nothing; it means treatments are chosen by benefit, burden and goals.
Dyspnea sensation does not equal hypoxemia and supplemental oxygen is not automatically the best symptom treatment.
assessment: Ask the patient's acceptable symptom level and priorities; assess severity, mechanism, prior response, function and caregiver capacity.
Review renal and hepatic function and opioid exposure before selecting or titrating analgesia.
workup: Only investigate when the result can lead to an intervention consistent with goals; avoid burdensome tests with no plausible benefit.
management: Use opioids proportionately for pain and selected refractory dyspnea, with bowel prophylaxis and toxicity monitoring.
Choosing Wisely Canada recommends against oxygen therapy solely for non-hypoxic dyspnea; use airflow, positioning, anxiety support and mechanism-specific therapy.
Treat constipation proactively with opioid therapy unless contraindicated.
medicationSafety: Renal failure increases toxicity risk for some opioid and metabolite choices; rotate or reduce appropriately.
Benzodiazepines are not first-line treatment for dyspnea itself but can be useful for selected severe anxiety or palliative sedation contexts under appropriate guidance.
redFlags: New catastrophic symptom the patient wants treated
Caregiver unable to safely manage at home
counselling: Explain expected medication effects, breakthrough dosing plan, constipation prevention and whom to call after hours.
followUp: Reassess soon after symptom-medication changes and ensure access to medications, equipment and 24-hour support when home care is the goal.
examTrap: Automatically ordering oxygen for severe dyspnea despite normal oxygenation while ignoring opioids and other symptom strategies.
oneLinePearl: In palliative care, treat suffering, not a monitor number.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Palliative Care Recommendations

title: Goals of Care and Advance Care Planning
bottomLine: Advance care planning identifies values and future decision-makers; goals-of-care conversations apply those values to the current clinical situation; consent is still required for specific treatments. Do not reduce these conversations to a CPR checkbox.
recognize: Serious-illness decisions are easier when prognosis, likely outcomes and patient priorities are discussed before crisis.
A capable patient's current wishes take priority over old documents that no longer reflect informed present choices.
differentiate: Code status is one treatment decision, not a complete plan of care.
A substitute decision-maker represents the incapable patient's applicable prior capable wishes, values and legal framework rather than simply choosing their own preference.
assessment: Ask what the patient understands, what matters most, unacceptable states or burdens, hopes and fears, and who should speak for them if they cannot.
Assess capacity for the specific decision and use interpretation and communication supports.
workup: No laboratory test determines goals of care; provide enough prognostic and clinical information to support informed decisions.
management: Make a recommendation that connects treatments to the patient's goals rather than offering a menu without guidance.
Document decisions and ensure they follow the patient across settings and revisit them after major health changes.
Before transferring a frail long-term-care resident to hospital, review goals and advance directives when urgent needs can potentially be met in place.
medicationSafety: Deprescribe preventive drugs whose burden or time-to-benefit no longer aligns with goals while preserving symptom-relief medicines.
redFlags: Unclear or conflicting substitute decision authority
Family demands that conflict with a capable patient's wishes
No documented plan during rapidly progressive illness
Care setting cannot meet urgent symptom or safety needs
counselling: Use plain language about what treatments can realistically achieve and allow uncertainty without abandoning recommendations.
followUp: Revisit goals after hospitalization, new diagnosis, functional decline or change in prognosis and communicate updates to the care team.
examTrap: Asking whether the patient wants everything done instead of explaining likely outcomes and linking treatment to the patient's values.
oneLinePearl: Goals tell you what matters; treatments are judged by whether they can get there.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Palliative Care and Long-Term Care Recommendations
